rationale: B wins because it has the adult supervision A lacks: it asks, "Whose side are you on here?" and separates pitchable angles from stories a reporter may write against Toast. A is strong in places, but it lets an underproved product page sneak in as "Restaurant payroll is uniquely messy. Toast is betting it can own that complexity." B still has one bad invented headline, but its proof gates and refusals are sharper strategy, not just tidy angle packaging.
gaps_in_A: "Restaurant payroll is uniquely messy" imports tipped-wage compliance detail — "tipped minimum wage variation by state, tip pooling rules, tip credits" — that the update did not give.
"Vertical SaaS found its margin — and it's not the software" turns one Toast fact into a category verdict before the comparable-company proof exists.
"opting out of its financial products comes with real friction" assumes lock-in and switching costs without adoption, contract, or switching evidence.
"Angles 1 and 2 ... are the most press-ready given public records access" overstates angle 2; the owner-power story needs named operators, fee amounts, and switching-cost proof.
gaps_in_B: "Toast reached profitability by selling loans, not hardware" is unsupported causality. The update says Toast reached profitability and says fintech is higher-margin; it does not say loans caused profit.
"an industry with well-known failure rates" imports outside context. Source it or cut it.
"comes out automatically through the same system that takes the payments" and "operator never writes a check" are plausible mechanics, not supplied facts. Product terms need to prove them.
"restaurant industry's lender" overstates the brief. We have 120,000 locations, not Toast Capital penetration or loan-book size.
